{
 "summary": "Includes the network type in `CService::GetKey()` by default so that addresses across different networks cannot produce identical key representations. Retains an optional network-less key calculation for `AddrMan` bucket positioning to preserve compatibility with existing `peers.dat` databases.",
 "problem": "Because `CService::GetKey()` previously only serialized address bytes and port without the network identifier, addresses on different networks (such as Tor and I2P) could produce identical key bytes. When used in per-peer Bloom filters tracking known addresses during addr relay, a node could falsely believe a peer already knows an address (e.g. `foo.onion` after sending `foo.i2p`), suppressing address relay.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"CService::GetKey() didn't include the network in the output. So in theory it would be possible for two IP2 and Tor addresses to have the same output from CService::GetKey(). This would have unexpected results when used in the per-peer bloom filter of known addresses - we may wrongfully assume that a peer knows foo.onion when we have sent to them foo.i2p.\"",
  "Net test `tor_i2p_same_bytes` demonstrates that an I2P address and Tor address constructed with matching 32-byte payloads collide under the old `GetKey()` method."

<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.
